Russia launched scores of drones at energy and civilian targets across Ukraine overnight on Wednesday, killing at least seven people in six regions, authorities said.
The attack involved 112 Shahed, Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, of which 88 were shot down or neutralised, Ukraine's air force said.
One person was killed in Bila Tserkva in Kyiv region, where the strike damaged critical infrastructure, an Epicentr shopping centre and a Nova Poshta postal branch, local authorities said.
One person was killed and seven injured in Kharkiv region after a strike hit a minibus on a highway, regional governor Oleh Synehubov said. Two people aged 76 and 69 were killed and another wounded in Sumy region.
Two people were killed in Odesa region on Tuesday evening — a 41-year-old and a 17-year-old — and one person was killed and three wounded in Zhytomyr region. Casualties were also reported in Chernihiv and Donetsk regions.
Russian forces struck a Naftogaz gas production facility in the Poltava region, the acting head of the company Serhiy Fedorenko said.
A fire broke out and the facility suspended operations. "This is not the first such attack and, unfortunately, not the last," Fedorenko said, adding that Russia was deliberately targeting gas production "to deprive Ukrainians of heat in winter."
Energy facilities in the Dnipropetrovsk region were also hit, triggering emergency power cuts across several districts.
A significant number of consumers lost power in Zaporizhzhia region, Zaporizhzhyaoblenergo head Andriy Stasevskyi said. More than 9,000 customers were left without electricity in Odesa region following Tuesday evening's attacks, regional governor Oleh Kiper said.
The energy company DTEK reported a large-scale strike on one of its thermal power plants, causing serious damage and forcing it to stop generating electricity. DTEK did not specify the location, noting it was the third large-scale strike on its plants in November.
Ukrainian drones simultaneously struck three Russian oil refineries overnight, hitting plants in Samara and Rostov regions, according to Ukrainian monitoring sources.
Two refineries in Samara region — the Kuibyshev and Syzran plants, both part of Rosneft — were struck, with fires breaking out at both facilities.
Regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed the attack but did not name the facilities, saying one person was killed, power had been cut in several districts and a number of schools would operate on an adjusted schedule.
Regional authorities said 145 drones were shot down over the Samara region. Euronews could not independently verify these claims.
The Syzran refinery has a processing capacity of 8.5 million tonnes of oil per year and produces petrol, diesel, aviation kerosene, fuel oil and bitumen.
The Kuibyshev refinery has a primary processing capacity of 8.8 million tonnes per year. Ukraine last struck the Syzran plant on 15 September. The Kuibyshev refinery was also struck that month.
The third refinery struck overnight was the Novoshakhtinsk plant in Rostov region. Regional governor Yuri Slyusar confirmed the attack, saying a combined strike of more than 50 drones and missiles lasted six hours before the plant suspended operations.
Russian oil refining volumes have fallen by an estimated 45% since late October, according to analysts.
Ukraine's General Staff also reported overnight strikes on the Savasleyka airbase in Nizhny Novgorod region, which it described as one of Russia's key aviation facilities and the base from which aircraft carrying Kinzhal missiles launch strikes on Ukrainian cities.
According to Kyiv's military, three MiG-31 and two Su-34 aircraft were damaged and would be unable to fly "for some time".
Ukraine destroyed a span of the road section of the Crimean Bridge last week, halting car traffic, though train services have been restored.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strike was a response to Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, describing deep strikes inside Russia as "long-range sanctions".
Ukraine attacked the bulk carrier Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday, claiming it transported military cargo. The following day it struck the Russian corvette Merkury in the Libyan port of Benghazi. Zelenskyy confirmed the warship had been sunk.
On Tuesday, Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened Ukraine with retaliation for its strikes on refineries and complained that Kyiv had not heeded calls from US President Donald Trump to halt attacks on oil processing facilities.
Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was prepared to stop striking Russian refineries only if Moscow halted its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

Ukraine has said it damaged five Russian military aircraft in an attack on Russia's Savasleyka airfield, 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow.
Three MiG-31 and two Su-34s aircraft were hit, Kyiv's General Staff said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed but that "there may be even better news to come". It did not elaborate on what weapons it had used to hit the airfield.
The airfield at Savasleyka, in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, has been a target for Ukraine for several years. It hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs.
The take-off of MiG-31s in particular frequently triggers nationwide alerts across Ukraine, as the Kinzhal missiles they carry have been known to hit large infrastructure and military targets and are difficult to shoot down.
Overnight, Kyiv also said it hit two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region some 800km (500 miles) from the front line – the latest in a series of long-range strikes which have dented Moscow's oil processing capacity.
"Did you repair them? We'll hit them again," the defence ministry in Kyiv said.
Samara region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said the night-time attacks had been "a true ordeal", with more than 145 drones shot down. One person was killed and several towns experienced power outages, Fedorishchev said.
Kyiv also said it had hit a radar system as well as fuel and logistics depots across Ukrainian territories currently occupied by Russia.
"Without fuel, military vehicles cannot move; without ammunition, artillery falls silent," the defence ministry said, adding that every successful hit meant Moscow could carry out fewer strikes.
Kyiv has developed a thriving weapons industry and Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets well beyond the front line have become commonplace in the years since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.
On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin called for a tightening of security measures across the country's energy facilities.
But he also argued that Russia had managed to stabilise its domestic fuel market without suffering "critical damage" and added that Moscow would "inevitably" retaliate against Kyiv.
Ukraine continues to come under daily attack. Ten people were killed across several regions between 24 and 25 November, while thousands are without power after Russian strikes on energy infrastructure.

President Donald Trump's administration on Wednesday reignited global trade tensions by proposing new tariffs on some of the largest US trading partners, including the EU, Japan and Taiwan. China could be slapped with a 20 percent tariff, a senior official said. The announcement came weeks after a cost-of-living crisis landed the Republicans a sweeping defeat in the US midterms.
The US on Wednesday unveiled proposed tariffs on 14 economies including the European Union and China , after a months-long probe into alleged excess production – the latest move by President Donald Trump to remake Washington's trade relationships.
The new tariffs are meant to discourage excessive manufacturing output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration says put US manufacturers at a disadvantage.
The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.
Read more Trump calls Supreme Court decision to strike down his tariffs 'deeply disappointing'
In a late-night call with reporters on Tuesday, a senior administration official provided details of the planned tariffs ahead of the release of a series of investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan . The official insisted on anonymity as a condition for discussing the reports before they were posted by the US Trade Representative's office.
The official stressed that the tariffs were still at the proposal stage and did not provide strict timelines on possible implementation.
The new levies target some of the United States' largest trading partners, including China, the European Union, India , Bangladesh , Cambodia , Indonesia , Japan , South Korea , Malaysia , Singapore , Switzerland , Taiwan , Thailand and Vietnam .
The US official made specific mention of China, for whom a 20 percent tariff is being proposed, the joint-highest for any economy.
In a separate announcement, the US Trade Representative's office also proposed additional tariffs on goods from Brazil , including aircraft, over alleged inaction on addressing US trade concerns.
Trump's tariffs have targeted Washington's friends and foes alike, and are part of a push in his second term to remake global trade by forcing countries to buy US products or produce their goods in his country.
The latest move offers some relief for partners that earlier signed tariff deals with the Trump administration, but it could still raise temperatures as the US president prepares to host G20 leaders in Miami in December.
"We don't expect this to create tension or rancor" at the G20 summit, the senior US official said. "We actually expect that we may be signing more agreements at the G20 in the wake of these announcements."

Responding to the announcement, the EU rejected the premise of the new tariffs and said it expected Washington to stick by a deal struck with Brussels last year.
"We will study the findings," European Commission spokesman Olof Gill told reporters in Brussels. "At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity," he said.
The EU has imposed trade restrictions to protect its industry amid overcapacity concerns, but these have been largely directed at China.
Brussels has long worried that excess production in China partially fuelled by state subsidies is resulting in a flood of low-cost imports undermining European manufacturers.
"The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action," Gill said of the US move.
The Commission would continue engaging with Washington on implementing a tariff deal struck in 2025 to cap Trump's duties on the bloc at 15 percent, he added.
"We expect any measure from this investigation to respect it in full, including when combined with existing duties," Gill said.
The duties could add further pressure on US businesses already squeezed by earlier tariffs, with firms now likelier to pass on costs to consumers already frustrated with the high cost of living .
Affordability was a key issue in recent midterm elections, which saw Trump's Republican Party swept out of power in both houses of Congress by Democrats.
Read more The economic drivers of US Republicans' rout at polls
US consumer inflation came in at 3.7 percent year-on-year in September, close to a three-year high as prices are pushed up by the effects of Trump's war on Iran, tariffs, and the massive AI investment boom.
US Federal Reserve policymakers, responsible for keeping inflation to a long-term two-percent target, say that most price effects of Trump's previous tariff rollout have passed through the economy – but any new levies could push prices up further.
The new tariffs are likely to come into effect in January at the earliest, the senior US official said.
Trump's latest duties come after an investigation the US Trade Representative started in March on excess manufacturing capacity and production.
The concern was whether other countries were taking actions deemed "unreasonable or discriminatory", and if they weighed on US commerce.
Trade lawyer Ryan Majerus told AFP that he expected this probe to be among "the most important" actions for the Trump administration, given its underlying concern that factories with excess capacity start operations abroad and "never get turned off, even if there's no demand".
This potentially leads to an oversupply of goods, depressed prices and a "hollowing out" of US manufacturing, he added.
The US determination is likely to face strong pushback from China and others, with Beijing long rejecting criticism that it relies too much on exports to boost its economy.
While the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's global tariffs in February, his sector-specific duties remain intact.
The new tariffs will not stack on top of those sector-specific tariffs on items like automobiles and steel, the senior US official said.
In July, Trump imposed a separate wave of tariffs on 60 economies , accusing them of insufficient action against forced labour.
For economies facing both the forced labor and excess production tariffs, the levies would not stack, the US official said. Instead, the higher rate of the two would prevail.

The US is aiming tariffs at 14 economies it accuses of using subsidies to help their factories overproduce.
The Trump administration has announced plans to impose new trade tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners, including China, the European Union and India, accusing them of flooding world markets with cheap goods. China faces the highest rates.
The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the duties on Wednesday following an eight-month investigation into what Washington calls “structural excess capacity”.
A senior US official told Reuters that USTR defines this as countries “promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles”, including through subsidies and other industrial policies.
The tariffs are the latest attempt to rebuild Trump’s sweeping import taxes that the US Supreme Court struck down in February.
The latest tariffs are being imposed under Section 301, part of a 1974 US trade law, which allows Washington to penalise countries it determines are treating US businesses unfairly. Trump used it to place large tariffs on Chinese goods during his first term, and those tariffs survived challenges in court.
The new tariffs are Trump’s latest attempt to bring back the “ Liberation Day ” tariffs he announced in April 2025 shortly after he began his second term in the White House. He imposed those under an emergency powers law but, in February this year, the Supreme Court ruled that the law did not allow him to impose trade tariffs.
“It’s supposed to be for international economic emergencies,” Dmitry Grozoubinski, a trade policy expert, said of the emergency law. “Tariffs are like taxes. You can’t really fight emergencies with mild taxes.”
The administration then used another law to put temporary 10 percent tariffs on trading partners in place, which ran out in July. It then replaced those with tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on 60 economies, which together supply almost everything the US imports. This time it used Section 301, arguing that those countries do not do enough to keep out goods made with forced labour.
Grozoubinski said Section 301 was designed to allow a president to hit back quickly at one country over one industry, not to tax almost every import. “The legislation is supposed to be a scalpel, and they used it like a flamethrower,” he said. “It is not meant to set the US tariff code, which is what this effectively did.”
The recent investigation into the “structural excess capacity” of trading partners began in March and covered industries from steel and cars to computer chips and solar panels. It examined government subsidies, wages suppressed by the state and the operations of state-owned companies.
Washington argues that this support enables foreign factories to sell their goods more cheaply around the world, undercutting American manufacturers and discouraging investment in the US. The senior official told Reuters that the new duties would not be added on top of the forced labour tariffs.
The investigation covered 16 economies, and tariffs have been proposed for 14 of them: China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. For now, Mexico and Norway, which were also investigated, have been spared.
The Trump administration views China as the biggest offender, pointing to its steel, aluminium, electric cars, household appliances and solar panels industries. Beijing rejects the accusation and says its exports are simply competitive. Washington also accuses Chinese companies of investing in Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia to bypass earlier US tariffs.
For the other economies, Washington pointed to the large trade surpluses of Germany and Ireland as evidence against the EU. It also singled out the car industries of China and Japan, Singapore’s computer chips and Norway’s fuel and seafood exports for criticism.
The senior official cited by Reuters did not provide rates for most countries ahead of their publication in the Federal Register. However, China will face the highest charges. The official said its proposed 20 percent excess capacity tariff would come on top of the roughly 25 percent in tariffs set during Trump’s first term. That keeps China above Vietnam, which also faces a proposed rate of 20 percent.
The official said the new duties would not break the tariff limits in trade deals the Trump administration has negotiated. According to earlier Reuters reporting, those include caps of 15 percent for the EU, Japan and South Korea, and 19 percent for Malaysia.
For China, the limit is 20 percent on tariffs imposed during Trump’s second term, under a trade truce with Beijing that expires on January 10.
India has no signed trade deal with the US. The two sides agreed the outline of one in February, but it was never finalised, and talks have dragged on for months. On November 14, Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar said a deal could be sealed soon.
Grozoubinski said the timing is significant. The proposal comes just weeks after midterm elections in which Trump’s Republican Party suffered unprecedented electoral losses, in which the cost of living and trade tariffs were major issues. A Reuters/Ipsos poll after the vote indicated that 62 percent of respondents would support efforts to scrap trade tariffs.
“One interpretation is, like, OK, they’re going to chill out on these tariffs, because basically every time they say the word tariffs, people remember that their costs are really high and get angrier,” Grozoubinski said. “This shows that at least on some level, they are still prepared despite the headwinds, to go ahead and push that button.”
Hisham Wahby, an independent political analyst, said the key question after the vote was whether Trump would “double down or pull back”. Days after the midterms, Trump named his longtime adviser, the hardline anti-immigration activist Stephen Miller, as White House chief of staff. Wahby said that “was a clear indicator he is going to double down”.
US importers are currently challenging the forced labour tariffs at the US Court of International Trade, and Grozoubinski called the reasoning behind them “incredibly dubious”. Accusations about subsidies, he said, will be easier to defend.
“One theory is maybe they’re going to impose these little tariffs now, but if their big tariffs on everybody on forced labour get cancelled, they can fall back and say, we’ve already done the investigation,” he said. In that case, he added, the new tariffs would “replace the tariffs that replaced the tariffs that replaced the tariffs that replaced the Liberation Day tariffs”.
The announcement also comes weeks before the US-China trade truce, agreed between President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jingping last year, runs out, while trade talks with India remain unfinished.
Wahby said the decision is hard to explain in economic terms. “He lost the midterms because of the cost of living, because of the price of goods. Small businesses were suffering,” he said. “Households are suffering, small businesses are suffering, and you double down on it.”
Grozoubinski said the new tariffs will certainly be challenged in court. However, he said they were likely to stay in place while the cases went on, because lower court rulings are usually appealed and put on hold. The emergency tariffs, he noted, stayed in force for months after the trade court first ruled against them, until the Supreme Court struck them down.
He added that these latest tariffs stand a better chance of surviving than earlier ones, because foreign subsidies are a more believable complaint than forced labour.
“There’s probably something there,” he said. If the investigation genuinely found unfair practices, he said, the Supreme Court may decide that Trump is within his rights and that it is up to Congress to stop him.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Wednesday declined to comment on reports in Russian and international news outlets that around 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the Ukraine war so far. The reports were based on hacked data from Russia's official statistics agency. Peskov said only the defence ministry can disclose figures and told reporters "not to pay attention to any other data".
The Kremlin on Wednesday declined to comment on reports that up to 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in its almost five-year-long offensive on Ukraine .
After analysing a trove of hacked data from Russia's official statistics agency, several Russian and international media outlets say Moscow's own data shows that between 470,000 and 700,000 soldiers have been killed in the war.
Russia has not given an official death toll among its army since September 2022, when it said almost 6,000 soldiers had been killed in the first six months of fighting – a figure widely seen as a large undercount even at the time.
Read more ‘Three times the Soviet-Afghan war’: New data sheds light on scale of Russian deaths in Ukraine
Asked about the new reports, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday: "The only entity that can officially disclose casualty figures is the defence ministry of the Russian Federation."
"I suggest not to pay attention to any other data," he added.
Earlier this month, hackers from two anti-Kremlin groups – the Belarusian Cyberpartisans and pro-Ukrainian outfit Silent Crow – published hundreds of thousands of records they said had been obtained by hacking the database of Russia's federal statistics agency, Rosstat.
By analysing the unpublished data on causes of death among Russian citizens over the last five years, several international outlets said the data showed the number of soldiers confirmed killed was close to 500,000.
A separate analysis by the banned independent Russian outlets Meduza and Mediazona said after including soldiers classified as "missing" – widely understood to have been killed but not yet registered – the toll could be as high as 700,000.

Russia has offered huge financial incentives to lure low-paid workers from poor regions to join the army.

North Korea has also sent tens of thousands of its soldiers to support Russia's army.

Operation in which one hostage-taker was killed ends daylong siege in Cartagena shopping centre, where 30 people were initially held
Colombian police have stormed a supermarket in one of the country’s most popular tourist cities, ending a daylong siege in which all the hostages were freed and one hostage-taker was killed.
Abelardo de la Espriella, the far-right president, travelled to the Caribbean port city of Cartagena to follow the final hours of negotiations and the tactical assault, in which special forces officers broke through blocked entrances and detonated stun grenades.
When masked and armed assailants stormed the supermarket at about 8.30am on Tuesday local time, 30 people including customers and employees were taken hostage, many of whom could be seen through windows with their hands and feet tied. Ten had already been released over the course of the day.
When, after 17 hours in captivity, the final 20 people were freed at about 1.30am on Wednesday, four of the hostage-takers were arrested and one was killed.
In a video posted outside the supermarket – about 6 miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls, which are visited by thousands of tourists every year – De la Espriella celebrated the end of the operation.
“One of the criminals was killed. They were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages; they rejected that opportunity and we acted forcefully,” he said. He appeared with a gun on his waist, as he has on several other occasions in public as part of his populist security rhetoric.
The president arrived in Cartagena late on Tuesday afternoon from Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he had been dealing with the aftermath of another attack on Monday night, when a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government.
More than 20 people were injured, and the president attributed the attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).
De la Espriella, however, denied that the supermarket hostage-taking had been carried out by a “terrorist group”, as he describes the groups involved in Colombia’s decades-long armed conflict, saying instead that those responsible were common criminals.
The president said they had tried to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle but, after being spotted by private security – who then alerted police – they took refuge in the supermarket.
As the lengthy negotiations continued into the night, police used water cannon to disperse dozens of onlookers who had gathered outside the supermarket.
Cartagena’s mayor, Dumek Turbay, told local media that when special forces stormed the supermarket, one of the hostage-takers resisted and was shot dead.
Some of the others tried to blend in with the hostages by removing their hoods and changing out of their black clothes into civilian clothing, he said.
According to Turbay, police then had to screen the hostages before eventually identifying the four who were arrested.
Supermarket employee Héctor Puello, who was taken hostage, told Caracol Radio that he had started his shift in the store’s bakery about two and a half hours before the gunmen arrived.
“First of all, I felt like I had come back to life because those armed men were mistreating us,” he said.
Another employee, Dayro Rafael Velázquez Castrillo, said that when he realised what was happening, he hid inside a cold-storage room with four other employees. “After four hours, we couldn’t stand the cold any longer and came out,” he said, at which point they were captured and taken hostage.
Commenting on what he called an “extraordinary” rescue operation, De la Espriella said his government was acting out of “the need to defend our people and go after all the criminals with an iron fist”.
The daylong hostage siege took place on a symbolic day for security in Colombia: the 10th anniversary of the country’s landmark peace accord with Farc guerrillas.
In office for just over three months, the president – previously a lawyer and businessman – is a fierce critic of the peace deal and has focused his government on returning to a strategy of full-on confrontation with criminal groups, breaking completely with the “total peace” plan of his predecessor, the leftist Gustavo Petro.
Although some indicators show slight improvements in areas such as homicides and kidnappings, recent days have been marked by a strong response from criminal groups: in addition to the car bombing, another guerrilla group carried out the first-ever drone attack on a departmental capital on Monday.
On Tuesday night, five departments were left without electricity, and De la Espriella said criminals used explosives to bring down power pylons.
“These criminal acts constitute the response of terrorist groups to the forceful offensive being carried out by the national government to restore order and security across the country,” he said.

A Canadian astronaut aboard the International Space Station is celebrating the birth of his third child from hundreds of miles above Earth.
Joshua Kutryk and his wife, Heather Kutryk, welcomed their daughter as the astronaut takes part in a six-month space mission that began in October, the Canadian Space Agency announced on Tuesday.
"Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives," said the couple in a statement shared by the agency.
Joshua Kutryk, currently on his first space mission, is just the fourth astronaut in history to miss the birth of a child while aboard the International Space Station.
"We are very proud of our growing family and are looking forward to getting our little crew of five all reunited."
In a statement, the couple said that Joshua's spaceflight was a "childhood dream" come true.
"We hope to show our children that big dreams are worth pursuing, that hard work and determination matter, and that with the support of family and a strong community, extraordinary things are possible," they said.
Prior to becoming an astronaut, Kutryk, from Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta, was a fighter pilot and a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force. He was recruited by the Canadian Space Agency in 2017.
Heather Kutryk said her family had been preparing for years prior to her husband's mission, calling it "a long time coming"
Kutryk was the only Canadian selected to be part of NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission, where four astronauts are conducting scientific experiments and testing new technologies in space.
The crew also includes two US astronauts, Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins, and one Russian astronaut, Sergey Teteryatnikov.
Before their take off on 1 October, Heather Kutryk told Canada's public broadcaster CBC News that her family had been preparing for years before the mission, saying it was "a long time coming".
Heather added that her pregnancy was "not exactly planned" but that it was "a great thing".
"I'm not that stressed out. I feel like we have a really good community. I feel well supported by both CSA and Nasa," she said.
In a separate interview with BBC's US news partner CBS News, Joshua Kutryk said he hopes his new child will look at her dad's mission as "making some sacrifice, taking some risk, but doing so in the name of public service and the name, in my case, for Canada."

Israel’s tech sector and economy have strong ties to chip giant Nvidia, which invests billions of dollars.
When Jensen Huang returned to lead the chip giant Nvidia this week after a scandal over his extramarital affairs, US President Donald Trump was not the only head of government to welcome his second coming.
Thousands of kilometres away, Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was celebrating too.
Huang once called Israel Nvidia’s “second home”, and Netanyahu reflected that feeling as he wrote on X: “Nvidia’s partnership with Israel’s tech sector has created enormous value for the company and for Israel’s innovation economy.”
“Continuity in Nvidia’s leadership is good news for that partnership and for the global AI industry,” Netanyahu added, referring to Huang’s reinstatement as CEO and president on Monday.
Global headlines have focused on Huang’s affairs, including with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset; his resignation’s implications for the AI industry; and the larger technology race between Washington and Beijing. His reinstatement at the company he cofounded has gone a long way to settle market jitters. Nvidia’s share price rocketed up by 30 percent on Monday.
But Huang’s return has also calmed nerves in Israel – arguably the country most impacted by Nvidia’s performance outside the United States as it hosts the US-based company’s largest overseas operations.
California-based Nvidia, the world’s most valuable semiconductor company with a market capitalisation of about $4 trillion, holds the key to the modern artificial intelligence revolution. Huang’s company holds an extraordinary near-90 percent share of the global market for GPUs – graphics processing units, which are specialised AI processors used in AI data centres.
Nvidia’s operations in Israel are its largest in research and development outside the US. It has doubled employees there in the past three years to 6,000 people across seven research and development centres in Yokne’am, Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, Ra’anana and Beersheba. It also has plans to build a major research and development campus in Kiryat Tivon near Haifa to accommodate up to 10,000 employees.
The Bank of Israel has estimated that Nvidia’s work in the country alone will add 2.2 percentage points of growth to Israel’s gross domestic product (GDP) in 2026, bringing it to 5.6 percent. Without Nvidia, that would be 3.4 percent growth, or 40 percent lower.
Next year, Nvidia is expected to add a further 2.4 percentage points to its GDP growth.
Nvidia paid about $1.29bn in taxes to Israel in its financial year that ended in January, according to its annual report. The company is projected to account for nearly 3 percent of Israel’s total state tax revenues in 2026, according to some estimates.
Huang’s resignation on November 12 initially rattled investors on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange (TASE) with the benchmark indices sliding after the announcement.
But by the end of the day, they had recovered. The TA-35 index finished 0.22 per cent higher at the close of the day while the broader TA-125 gained 0.07 per cent. The BlueTech Global Index, which tracks technology companies, fell 0.15 per cent.
The Haaretz newspaper reported, however, that officials at Israel’s Ministry of Finance were concerned about the potential consequences for the Israeli economy of turmoil – and particularly Huang’s exit – at Nvidia.
On Monday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog congratulated Huang on his return, noting “his deep appreciation to Huang for his continued support for Israel and for his commitment to strengthening the connection between Nvidia and Israel”.
Herzog’s office said Huang told the president that he was “moved by the message and that he intends to make the most of the second chance he has been given”.
Nvidia is helping fuel Israel’s economic machine during its genocidal war on Gaza, pogroms by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and the occupation of southern Lebanon.
But Israel is also returning strong numbers for the company.
The root of the tech giant’s relationship with the country can be traced back to Nvidia’s acquisition of Mellanox, an Israeli company that supplies computer networking products, in April 2020 for nearly $7bn. That acquisition was central to Nvidia’s success.
Nvidia was already able to make powerful engines that process AI workloads, but a single GPU cannot handle that workload and needs to exchange information with other GPUs.
Mellanox made the networking infrastructure that allows those engines to work together at a fast pace, creating the foundational structure of a data centre.
Nvidia’s networking business, built around Mellanox, generated more than $21bn in revenues in the third quarter of 2026. That’s about 18 percent of Nvidia’s total quarterly revenue.
At the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas in January, Huang spoke about Israel’s role in the development of key Nvidia chips.
“Nvidia’s BlueField-4 DPU and three networking components – the ConnectX-9 SuperNIC, NVLink 6 Switch and Spectrum-6 Ethernet Switch – all came out of Israel. So four out of six chips came out of Israel,” he said, praising the employees in Israel.
“Pretty amazing and maybe next time, six out of six chips,” Huang added.
A review by the American Friends Service Committee, a group that won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1947 partly for its work rescuing and providing relief to Jews during the Holocaust, has found that the Israeli military uses multiple Nvidia products.
Several purchases of Nvidia products were disclosed by the Israeli Ministry of Defence during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, a report by the group last year noted.
“They include products that are designed for AI applications, like Jetson cards and DGX,” it said, adding that since the public database only records unclassified contracts, “this likely represents only part of the full scale of the military’s usage of Nvidia products and services.”
Israel has made extensive use of AI systems in the Gaza war – including those known as The Gospel, Lavender and Where’s Daddy? – to track and target Palestinians at an unprecedented scale, the group said, adding that Nvidia “could therefore be potentially implicated in these war crimes”.
The Nvidia Jetson TX2 AI processor is also reportedly integrated into Elbit Systems’ Lanius drones, which Israel has used to kill Palestinian civilians in Gaza.

China has launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with a Pakistani astronaut on board, the first time a foreign national has flown to its Tiangong space station.
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, lifted off on Wednesday morning with Chinese crewmates Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China.
Hours earlier, crowds gathered for a send-off ceremony, many filming on their phones.
Following the launch, the capsule separated from its rocket and reached its planned orbit.
It is the first joint flight of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's crewed space programme.
Thousands of kilometres away, Pakistanis watched the ascent on television at home and in restaurants, chanting slogans in praise of God and of Pakistan-China friendship. Scientists at the national space agency's headquarters followed the launch live.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called the mission a source of national pride and an inspiration for the country's youth.
"This is not just one astronaut's journey, but the journey of 240 million Pakistanis," he wrote on X. He thanked Beijing for including a Pakistani astronaut and said the flight extended the two countries' close ties into space.
Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, speaking to reporters at the agency, thanked President Xi Jinping, China's leadership and its scientists and engineers, and said he hoped the flight would be the start of broader cooperation.
Asked whether Pakistan could one day send astronauts on its own, he replied: "Certainly that day will come."
Iqbal said Ali carried the Pakistani flag on his uniform, lifting his compatriots' hopes and technological ambitions into orbit. "The sky is no longer our limit; it is our launching pad," he said, calling the mission an inspiration for young Pakistanis hoping for careers in science and technology.
The flight stems from an agreement the two countries signed in February 2025. The Chinese media reported that the crew will carry out more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests.
Ali, who is on a short-term mission, will run an experiment on photosynthetic cyanobacteria before returning to Earth aboard Shenzhou 23. Ali and Wu are making their first spaceflight. Tang has flown twice before and is set to become the first astronaut to board Tiangong three times, according to state broadcaster CCTV.
At a press conference on Tuesday, Tang said differences in language, culture and psychology had made training together harder, but that the effort was paying off.
Ali showed as much by speaking Mandarin and citing a line of Chinese poetry about climbing higher to see farther. "It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights," he said.
Switching to English, Ali said he hoped cooperation would grow from one astronaut on one flight to multiple joint missions and eventually to the Moon, Mars and beyond.
China is preparing to land astronauts on the Moon by 2030. The United States is widely seen as its main rival, with NASA aiming to put astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

The president’s comments came after pressuring Nvidia’s board to reinstall Huang as CEO despite lawmakers’ concerns over national security
Donald Trump said on Tuesday he would be open to pardoning Jensen Huang , the recently reinstalled Nvidia CEO , for potential crimes but didn’t think it would be necessary.
“It’s always an option, I guess,” the US president told the New York Post in an interview. “But I don’t think it’ll be necessary.”
Trump’s comments came after he intervened in Nvidia’s leadership drama and put pressure on the tech company’s board to reinstall Huang as the CEO despite other lawmakers’ concerns over whether Huang posed a national security risk for having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Huang is expected to testify to congressional committees in the coming weeks about Nvidia’s chip exports, Huang’s alleged affair and the US government’s role in having Nvidia reinstate Huang as CEO.
“I think I want [Huang] to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know, a very smart person,” Trump told the New York Post.
Huang has not been formally accused of any crime, and Todd Blanche, the US attorney general, told reporters on Tuesday that no evidence indicated Huang committed a crime.
“To the extent that … the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this, that is, that’s just not, that’s something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true,” Blanche said.
At the same time, Blanche did not confirm whether the justice department had conducted a thorough investigation into Huang, instead saying law enforcement agents “looked into” the situation.
Yet days earlier, Trump told CNBC that his administration had done “a pretty good investigation” to exonerate Huang.
But lawmakers from both sides of the aisle have questions about the US government’s determination
John Curtis, a Republican who sits on the Senate commerce committee, wrote on X : “Nvidia’s board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk. I have some questions. Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?”
Pete Ricketts, a Republican who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, wrote on X on Monday, “Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress. It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips.”
John Kennedy, a Republican on the Senate banking committee, told Fox News that he wanted to know more about Huang’s alleged affair for national security purposes.
“I got no interest; it’s not my place if Mr Huang wants to be a feral, if he wants to cheat on Mrs Huang. It is my interest, though, if he was having sex with a Chinese spy,” Kennedy said.
“The Trump Administration needs to explain what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials to support Huang’s reinstatement,” Elizabeth Warren, top Democrat on the Senate banking committee, wrote on X on Monday.
Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat on the Senate homeland security committee, raised concerns about whether Trump “knew about the potential compromise with the alleged Chinese spy influencing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang” and “did nothing about it”.

Senegal's football federation reacted to the Cas verdict on social media with a picture of the side lifting the Afcon trophy alongside the caption "again and always champions of Africa"
That was the initial reaction of Senegal football federation (FSF) president Abdoulaye Fall to the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) to reinstate the West Africans as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champions.
The Teranga Lions beat Morocco 1-0 in January's final but were stripped of the title in March by a Confederation of African Football (Caf) appeals board, which imposed a 3-0 forfeit after they walked off the pitch in protest at a penalty awarded against them when the game was goalless.
Following a hearing in Lausanne in October, a three-man Cas panel unanimously overturned that ruling by Caf, effectively judging that the decisions taken by referee Jean-Jacques Ndala in restarting the match and playing it to a conclusion were final.
Morocco's football federation (FRMF), however, says it will "pursue all available legal avenues to challenge the decision".
The North Africans could yet take their fight to the Swiss Federal Court.
Those in Senegal have celebrated the return of the title, while several legal experts have backed the Cas verdict.
Senegal's talisman Sadio Mane, who was named player of the tournament at Afcon 2025, said the ruling "fills us with joy".
The 34-year-old former Liverpool man thanked his team-mates and Senegal staff as well as the whole Senegalese nation at home and abroad.
"Your faith in us gave us strength during the most difficult moments. This victory is yours, too," he said in a statement on social media.
Senegal captain Kalidou Koulibaly, who missed the final through injury, echoed that sentiment.
"Some victories are won on the pitch, while others are won in the heart of a people," he said in a post on Facebook.
"Long before this verdict, there was you - your prayers, your flags in the windows, your fervour, and the pride that unites us all: the pride of the people of Teranga."
Pape Gueye, the man who scored the extra-time winner in Rabat, described the Cas decision as "an immense relief".
"Senegal and Morocco are brotherly nations; may our shared passion for football continue to bring us closer together," Mane said.
Gueye added: "Beyond football, the respect and fraternity between our two peoples remain what matters most. Let's hold on to that.
Morocco's main complaint is that Articles 82 and 84 of Afcon tournament regulations - which were implemented by the Caf appeals board in March - were not followed by Cas.
Article 82 states that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" it shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition".
Article 84 then states a 3-0 forfeit should be imposed on a team which is eliminated in such circumstances.
"There [are] football rules that should have been applied by the referee," former Morocco international Hassan Kachloul told BBC Sport.
"When the Senegalese players left the pitch, the game should have been over."
The FRMF registered its "surprise" at the Cas decision and said that the panel "failed to account for the stance recently established" by the International Football Association Board (Ifab), the game's ultimate lawmakers, and world governing body Fifa regarding players leaving the field of play without the referee's permission.
However, Ifab only updated its laws in April - three months after the Afcon final - to state that a referee may send off any player who leaves the field when protesting a decision.
Moroccan football journalist Jalal Bounouar says his compatriots are "frustrated and disappointed" by the ruling.
"The main reason is that Caf's appeal board had already applied Article 82 and 84 of the competition regulations which considered Senegal to have forfeited the match," he told Newsday on the BBC World Service.
"Many Moroccans feel the decision by Cas has ignored the importance of these rules. From the Moroccan perspective, the referee should have taken stronger disciplinary action.
"We feel that our team was put in a difficult situation and that the final was not managed fairly."
Cas has a long-standing practice of following what has been called the 'field of play' doctrine.
It refrains from "reviewing decisions taken on the playing field by referees for applying the rules of the game, unless there is evidence that those rules were applied arbitrarily or in bad faith".
"The primary argument was that the referee is the master of the decision on the pitch," said Serge Vittoz, a member of the FSF's legal team.
Raymond Hack, both a former head of disciplinary at Caf and a former arbiter at Cas, said the judgement was the "correct verdict".
"What everyone seems to forget - and whilst there may be contradictory information in Article 82 and 84 - decisions taken by the referee during the match are final," the South African told the BBC World Service.
"Only the referee can start a game. Only a referee can end a game."
For former Nigeria striker Daniel Amokachi, an Afcon winner in 1994, the Cas ruling is "the right decision".
"At the end of the day, the man in charge of the match (Ndala) restarted the game, the game ended," he said.
Caf president Patrice Motsepe has repeatedly said his organisation will respect and adhere to Cas' decision
Caf has already tightened its own regulations to avoid a repeat.
But Algerian sports journalist Maher Mezahi says the continental governing body still needs to salvage its image.
"How many times have we seen Caf's legal institutions, whether it be the disciplinary board or the appeals committee, come up with these decisions that we all find ridiculous," he said.
"They end up being challenged at Cas and eventually they get overturned.
"We have to rebuild trust in Caf's own judicial bodies because it is a little bit humiliating and degrading and it brings the entire reputation of the confederation into disrepute."
The 2027 Afcon is scheduled to take place in June and July next year, and Senegal and Morocco were among the first qualifiers earlier this month.
Kachloul says the next tournament provides a chance to draw a definitive line under what happened in Rabat in January.
"This event, wherever you look at it on the Senegalese side or Moroccan side, doesn't look good at all," the one-time Aston Villa midfielder said.
"They are lucky to have another [Afcon] tournament in six months to redeem themselves and to paint a better picture of African football.
"The best way to prove that you're the best is to go back on the pitch and let the football talk."

The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled that Senegal were the rightful winners of the 2025 African Cup of Nations.
Senegal reinstated as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations winners over Morocco
The president of the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF), Abdoulaye Fall, has denied Moroccan allegations that he had “contact” with a Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) arbitrator who ruled that Senegal were the rightful winners of the 2025 African Cup of Nations.
The Moroccan federation (FRMF) alleged after Tuesday’s ruling there had been “contact” between Fall and German arbitrator Ulrich Haas, one of the three CAS panel members, 48 hours before they decided “unanimously” to award the trophy to Senegal.
“That is absolutely false. I have never had any exchange with any member of CAS,” said Fall on private television channel TFM on Wednesday.
“It surprised and astonished me that such accusations could even be made. I have never been in contact with anyone in connection with this procedure.”
In January, Senegal won a chaotic final 1-0 after extra-time.
But two months later, the Confederation of African Football (CAF) sensationally overturned the result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory, and the title, after many Senegalese players walked off the pitch in protest at a penalty given to the hosts with the game still goalless.
The CAF Appeals Committee had justified its decision to overturn the result and declare Morocco champions based on Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON Regulations.
Those state that if a team “refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee, it shall be considered [loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition”.
However, the Senegal players eventually returned to the pitch and the final carried on.
The three-person CAS panel therefore considered the referee’s decision to restart the final showed “the conditions for resuming the match had been met”, and that articles 82 and 84 were therefore “not applicable in this case”.
The Moroccan federation has the option of lodging an appeal with the Swiss Federal Supreme Court, which does not rule on the merits of the case, but intervenes in procedural matters.
texts.https://www.theguardian.com/football/202:
After African football was dragged into needless disrepute the next step is to tackle two key areas of governance
A journey of 310 days and three legal proceedings to confirm two things we know – that Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 to win the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and, most importantly, that the decision of a referee remains final and sacrosanct – has produced the longest, most comical and embarrassing Afcon final in the tournament’s 69-year history.
As the Confederation of African Football (Caf) executive committee member Samir Sobha told the Guardian, the decision of the organisation’s appeals board in March to overturn Senegal’s victory and award the title to Morocco, prompting a legal charade ended by the court of arbitration for sport’s verdict on Tuesday , was a “big joke” that brought Caf and the Afcon into needless disrepute.
“Correcting one injustice with another cannot be considered an acceptable response, either from a sporting or an ethical standpoint,” Sobha said. “Football is founded on core values: fairness, merit and the truth of what happens on the field. Awarding a title outside these principles, even when supported by regulatory provisions, undermines the credibility of the competition and damages the integrity of the game.
“Rather than restoring balance, such a choice risks intensifying frustrations and calls for a deeper reflection on how to safeguard fairness and uphold the honour of African football.”
Managing the huge reputational damage from the crisis over the past 10 months has been arguably the biggest governance test for the five-year Caf presidency of the South African billionaire Patrice Motsepe.
In a frustrated, exasperated moment, he admitted he was “sick and tired” of it all, navigating the treacherous diplomatic minefield of wounded Moroccan and Senegalese feelings, while reiterating his neutrality and belief in the integrity of the judicial process to bring the dispute to a just end.
The Cas resolution of the dispute compels Caf to carry out a desperately needed and long overdue task: the root-and-branch reform of its justice system, particularly the appeals board chaired by the Nigerian judge Roli Harriman.
The Cape Verdean Faustino Varela Monteiro, the board’s vice-chair, is a notable, honourable exception, standing for the correct legal position in his dissenting judgment.
The appeals board needlessly overturned the verdict of Caf’s disciplinary committee, which struck the right balance of upholding the result of the final while imposing fines and bans on the Senegal team for the egregious act of disrupting the match, and in so doing exposed its acute lack of understanding of the critical role it is duty-bound to play in the dispensation of football justice.
“You are right,” says a Caf executive committee member about the need to dissolve the appeals board and reconstitute it with jurists possessing the knowledge needed to restore confidence in the African football justice system.
Ensuring that politically exposed people are no longer members of a reconstituted appeals board is also imperative, if confidence in the impartiality of its verdicts is to be restored. No federation president should have a place on it. The presence of Moez Nasri, the president of the Tunisian Football Federation, strips it of credibility, as Motsepe acknowledged when I pointed this out to him in March.
But the poor quality of Jean-Jacques Ndala Ngambo’s refereeing of the Afcon final and Safari Olivier Kabene’s equally bad chairing of Caf’s referees committee – whose selection of match officials was responsible for the inadequate quality of game management throughout the last tournament – remain the proverbial elephants in the governance room.
When I asked a high-ranking Caf official why Ngambo has not faced a disciplinary hearing for his management of the final, he claimed its hands were tied by the Cas judicial process. That excuse expired on Tuesday.
Ngambo’s decision to allow a restart of the game, after Senegal illegally walked out for about 15 minutes in protest against a penalty awarded to Morocco, was a deeply questionable, some would say unacceptable, use of his discretionary powers, which should have leaned towards a declaration of match abandonment, with Morocco being declared the winners.
That said, the referee’s earlier failure to award Senegal what appeared to be a clear goal, subsequently giving a penalty to Morocco in second-half stoppage time, was the trigger for the chaos.
Ngambo’s lack of fortitude and experience to cope with the demands of an Afcon final is an indictment of the committee that picked the wrong man to handle it. And Kabene is responsible for that. “We have to do a clearout of the referees committee,” says a member of the Caf executive committee.
It is a situation in sharp and sad contrast to the world-class officiating at the 2024 Afcon in Côte d’Ivoire, under the competent general management of the Ivorian Noumandiez Doué, who would be the ideal person to restore sanity.
But after the shabby way he was treated, losing his job while on assignment at the last Championship of African Nations for domestic-based players in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania – the countries staging the 2027 Afcon – it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than it would be to convince him to return to his old job.
With just over eight months to the next Afcon and 20 months to the 2028 tournament, yet to have a designated host, Caf’s governance and organisational challenges are far from over.
The last two Afcons of Motsepe’s presidency, which ends in March 2029, will be decisive in shaping his legacy.
texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art:
Raheem Sterling has scored 123 goals in 396 Premier League appearances and provided 65 assists
Raheem Sterling grew up a stone's throw from Wembley Stadium, and went on to start a European Championship final for England there.
At his peak, the four-time Premier League winner was earning £325,000 a week at Chelsea .
"Raheem is a huge player with a huge influence in the last few years in English football," said then Blues boss Thomas Tuchel when he signed a 27-year-old Sterling in a £50m deal in 2022.
"He is at the perfect age to take responsibility around the younger players that we have and be an example.
"He just needs to do what he did over the last few years and he will be a huge asset for us."
Sterling enjoyed a 10-year England career, also played for Liverpool , Manchester City and Arsenal , and commanded combined transfer fees of about £100m.
But his career at the top level looks to be in the balance at the age of 31 after he was handed a 12-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months, for dangerous driving. Sterling has also been disqualified from driving for two years and ordered to carry out 100 hours of unpaid work.
At an earlier hearing in September, Sterling admitted dangerous driving on a motorway before crashing a Lamborghini on 28 May.
The crash caused "substantial" damage to his car and all four wheels, which prevented him from driving further, the court heard.
Sterling also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis.
Born in Kingston, Jamaica, he was just two when his father was shot dead.
His mother, Nadine, was determined to give her children a safer environment to live in. She moved to England to lay a path for Sterling and his sister to join her once she had found a home and finished her education, while cleaning bathrooms and changing bedsheets in hotels to earn extra money.
Sterling grew up on a housing estate in Neasden, north-west London, and spent part of his education at Vernon House, where teachers attempted to help the football-obsessed youngster with behavioural problems.
In an interview with the Players' Tribune , external in 2018, Sterling said: "I was so naughty that they kicked me out of primary school. I just didn't like to listen to anyone but my mum. That was my problem."
He was 10 when teacher Chris Beschi told him: "If you carry on the way you're going, by the time you're 17 you'll either be playing for England or in prison."
Sterling would grow to become one of the standout English attacking talents of his generation.
Raheem Sterling: From school struggles to a class of his own
On 14 November 2012 - aged 17 years and 342 days - Sterling made his England debut on the night his Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard won his 100th cap in a 4-2 defeat by Sweden in Stockholm.
Sterling would go on to make 81 more appearances for his country, scoring 20 goals.
He featured at three World Cups - 2014, 2018 and 2022 - and two European Championships. He was one of the standout players as England reached the Euro 2020 final at Wembley, where they were beaten by Italy.
Sterling was now at the peak of his career - the former Queens Park Rangers youngster, who has a tattoo on his forearm of a young boy holding a football looking up at the Wembley arch, named in the team of the tournament by Uefa.
Liverpool had signed a 15-year-old Sterling from QPR for £600,000 in February 2010.
He made his senior Reds debut two years later and became the second-youngest goalscorer in their history - behind Michael Owen - when he scored the winner against Reading in October 2012 at the age of 17.
In 2015, Sterling joined Manchester City in a deal worth up to £49m, making him the most expensive English player at the time.
He had been under contract at Anfield until 2017 but turned down a new deal to move to Liverpool 's rivals, with City boss Manuel Pellegrini describing the 20-year-old as "one of the best attacking players in world football".
Sterling went on to score 131 goals in 339 appearances in all competitions during seven successful years at Etihad Stadium.
As well as four Premier League titles, he helped City win five League Cups, one FA Cup and one Community Shield.
It was while he was at City, in 2021, that Sterling became an MBE in the Queen's Birthday Honours for his services to racial equality in sport.
"I am grateful to have been recognised," he said. "But my priority is to try to help to educate society and myself. I'm learning every day."
After City came the move to Chelsea , where his career began to stall.
Tuchel, now England manager, was sacked two months after signing Sterling, who made just 45 Premier League starts for the Blues over four years.
Off the pitch, he launched a scholarship fund aimed at closing the gap in the number of black British students who go to university.
He spent 18 months as a member of Chelsea 's so-called 'bomb squad' , and a season-long loan to Arsenal in 2024-25 proved largely unsuccessful.
Sterling: If you grew up in a certain area you feel like there's limits
As well as his success on the field, Sterling has made headlines off it too.
In 2015, when he was 20, reports began to surface about his behaviour away from the game.
Sterling was pictured apparently inhaling nitrous oxide and was also photographed smoking a shisha pipe.
That prompted then Liverpool boss Brendan Rodgers to warn Sterling he would "look back in 20 years and wonder what he was doing".
Sterling also made headlines while on duty for England at the 2018 World Cup in Russia.
The Sun ran a story titled "Raheem shoots himself in the foot" as pictures emerged of a tattoo of an M16 assault rifle on his leg.
Sterling explained on social media: "When I was 2 my father died from being gunned down to death I made a promise to myself I would never touch a gun in my life time. I shoot with my right foot so it has a deeper meaning."
The incident led to a widespread discussion in the UK about the treatment of black athletes in the media, with comparisons drawn between how Sterling's life was covered compared to others.
Sterling spoke out a number of times on the issue and wider racism in society, which was reflected in him being made an MBE.
Five years after his MBE, Sterling's career has stalled. He has not played since appearing for Feyenoord on 17 May, after agreeing a short-term move to the Netherlands.
Eleven days after that game, he was arrested after crashing a Lamborghini near the M3 in Hampshire.
Listen: From Wembley schoolboy to playing for England at Wembley
Sterling was riding the crest of a wave when he moved from Manchester City to Chelsea in the summer of 2022 for £50m.
His medal cabinet was already fit to burst with 10 major trophies under Guardiola and, alongside Harry Kane, he was arguably England's most important player for then head coach Gareth Southgate.
Tuchel viewed Sterling as his number one target that summer and Chelsea 's new ownership - Behdad Eghbali and Todd Boehly - delivered as the club entered the post-Roman Abramovich era.
Two months later, Tuchel was sacked and Graham Potter was in situ.
It is, of course, senseless to suggest the troubles Sterling has had on and off the pitch in recent years are simply down to the sacking of Tuchel in 2022.
But speak to those close to Sterling and they will explain Tuchel was among the key factors behind the winger's decision to swap Manchester for west London.
He was captivated by Tuchel's vision, not only for the team, but his role in it.

The strike caused extensive damage to the Abu al-Ouf family's apartment
An Israeli air strike in the Gaza Strip has killed a senior Hamas security official and three members of his family, according to local doctors and the Hamas-run interior ministry.
Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters died when their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City was bombed at dawn, the ministry said.
The Israeli military said Abu al-Ouf was a "terrorist" and that he was eliminated "to remove the threat he posed".
On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.
Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
Wednesday's strike in Shati caused extensive damage to the Abu al-Ouf family's apartment.
Photos showed the exterior wall and several interior walls were destroyed, with rubble and broken furniture left scattered across the floor.
An interior ministry statement said that Abu al-Ouf was killed along with his wife Noura, 41, and their daughters Yusra, 15, and Jana, 13.
It condemned the attack as a "heinous crime" and accused Israel of targeting security personnel in Gaza "in an effort to spread chaos within Palestinian society".
Hamas's internal security service is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting the group's infrastructure and rooting out informants.
Israel's military said in a statement that Abu al-Ouf was a "significant figure" who had served as "a key source of expertise" in efforts to restrict Israeli counter-terrorism operations in Gaza.
"His elimination is a blow to the apparatus's leadership capabilities and follows yesterday's elimination of his commander," it added.
On Tuesday, an Israeli drone strike in western Gaza City killed Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service.
He had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid in Gaza City by Israeli special forces.
Near daily Israeli strikes continue in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreed in October last year.
At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

Muhammad Zeeshan Ali – the first Pakistani to reach orbit – greeted with Chinese ‘space handshake’ at Tiangong station
China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation.
Floating through a hatch to enter Tiangong, Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali grinned broadly as he was embraced by the onboard crew in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”.
Tiangong, completed in 2022, is the jewel in the crown of China’s space programme. The government has invested billions into its celestial ambitions in recent years to catch up with the US and Russia, two of the five partners involved in the ISS along with Europe, Japan and Canada. After 25 years of continuous occupation, the ISS is set to cease operations from 2030, according to Nasa.
On Wednesday China’s president, Xi Jinping, told his Pakistani counterpart that Beijing was “willing to work with all countries … to uphold the banner of the peaceful use of outer space”.
Ali was part of the crew of Shenzhou 24, the most recent iteration of the series of missions that rotate astronauts in the space station every six months. He is the first Pakistani to reach orbit.
Blaine Curcio, the managing director at Orbital Gateway Consulting, told the Guardian: “Sending another country’s astronaut to space is a major undertaking. Pakistan is putting a lot of trust into Beijing by having him fly into space on a Chinese-built rocket.
“There are also considerations related to security: Ali is getting detailed insights into China’s crewed space programme … It makes China better prepared to do it again, and also makes it clear to other countries that China is open to this type of collaboration.”
Space cooperation between China and Pakistan dates back to the early 1990s. China has launched Pakistani satellites, and a Pakistani-built rover ‌is due to fly on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028.
Shenzhou 24 blasted off from the Jiuquan launch centre in north-west China against a pink-tinged dawn sky on Wednesday and first docked with the space station three and a half hours later.
Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan air force pilot and payload specialist, will conduct experiments including one cultivating microalgae as a potential food and another testing the effects of spaceflight on quinoa seeds. To prepare for the mission, he ​trained for seven months in Beijing, including taking intensive Chinese-language classes.
At a press conference the day before the launch, Ali recited a line from a classical Chinese poem. Commander Tang Hongbo told reporters that differences in language and culture had made learning to work together more challenging but that the effort had paid off.
Ali will not stay for the six-month term usually demanded of Tiangong astronauts. Instead, he will return to Earth with two of the Shenzhou 23 crew while its commander, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain to reach another milestone – the first full-year stay in space by a Chinese astronaut.
Beijing’s accelerated achievements in the skies have spooked its rivals. China is the third country to put humans in orbit and it has landed robotic rovers on Mars and the moon, where it hopes to send crewed missions within the next decade.
In racing to the moon before 2030, Beijing is competing with the US’s Artemis programme . The US has excluded China from the ISS since 2011, banning Nasa from collaborating with Beijing. In 2025, Nasa went further by blocking Chinese citizens from its facilities altogether.
US lawmakers have moved to try to extend the life of the ISS, citing China’s “permanent human presence in low Earth orbit” through Tiangong. Progress on turning that proposal into law has been slow. Nasa has said that after the ISS it will be “one of many customers in a robust commercial marketplace in low Earth orbit”.
The ISS was heralded as a symbol of post-cold war cooperation, but renewed cooperation with Russia seems “unlikely”, said Andrew Jones, a journalist specialising in China’s space programme.
While Tiangong is smaller than the ISS, China is understood to be preparing to double its size, “likely with the end of the ISS in mind”, Jones added. “These developments could allow China to expand its international engagement, and potentially space tourism. With the ISS nearing the end of its life and the future of western commercial space stations uncertain, China could for a time have the only permanently crewed outpost in low Earth orbit.”
China has long signalled its interest in developing Tiangong as an international hub. China Manned Space Agency documents published in coordination with the UN outline “resources for international cooperation” onboard the station. European and Chinese astronauts previously trained together with a view to a visit to Tiangong, but that cooperation ended for political and budgetary reasons, Jones said.
Curcio said he would expect countries such as Brazil and Egypt to seek out opportunities to send astronauts on Chinese missions. He added: “I think when the ISS is retired, if there is no western replacement (government or commercial), then yes, we may eventually see European or other ISS-involved countries – like Russia – send astronauts to Tiangong.”

Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, after its owners failed to find a buyer to keep it in business.
The retailer's shops and distribution centres will remain open and continue to trade during the administration process with the business likely to be broken up and some of its stores sold off to rival retailers.
Poundland's US owners held talks with several bidders over a last-minute rescue deal, but no agreement was reached.
Poundland boss Barry Williams said in a note to staff that the board had "no alternative but to take this decision", but was making it with "sincere sadness and intense regret".
He said the US owners Gordon Brothers had removed "all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts" on 27 October, and adequate funds had not been released since then to keep the business solvent.
"Under these circumstances, it is impossible for the board of directors to see how Poundland can continue to operate as a going concern," he added.
Kelvin Blake, pictured at a protest in Walsall, has worked for Poundland for 25 years
Kelvin Blake, 62, who has worked for the firm for 25 years, and whose partner has been there 29 years, said he was feeling "down, depressed", and because of his age, feared he would not find a job elsewhere.
"We didn't want it, but it's come so now we've just got to face it and see what the future holds.
"My income's gone," he added. "Obviously, we'll be working until we're told to leave."
Alix Partners, which has been appointed as administrator, said they would look at all options for the business, "including sales of the business and its assets, either in whole or part".
"We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved - customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues," they said.
Gordon Brothers has been criticised over how it handled a potential sale of Poundland, with accusations the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off the chain's 600 shops and stock piecemeal after running it into the ground.
Gordon Brothers, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied such claims.
On the funding question, Gordon Brothers said it had loaned the firm £85m over a year to help save it from insolvency.
But insiders critical of the US firm have said it stands to make its loans back and more from the insolvency process.
Previously, Gordon Brothers netted millions from liquidating the stock of fashion retailer LK Bennett, and in insolvency fees.
Labour MP Liam Byrne told the BBC the House of Commons' Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee will recall Gordon Brothers before Parliament.
He said: "I am really worried that a 'greed is good' approach to business by its owners has forced [Poundland] into an administration."
He added the committee wants to know "how much money they're ripping out and crucially, how do we make sure, as a country, that we don't have this kind of scenario unfold again".
Gordon Brothers said on Wednesday that despite the Poundland management bringing about a turnaround over the past year, the firm was "still vulnerable" to inflation and any downturn in sales or profit margin, and it had faced "several years of instability".
A spokesperson added the firm's "thoughts are with Poundland colleagues".
It said it had stepped in to take over the retailer in 2025 when it was struggling, and when "no-one else was willing to finance the business".
One of the central stumbling blocks in negotiations to keep the business afloat was a shareholder loan Gordon Brothers inherited when it bought the business for less than £1 last year.
Gordon Brothers was owed £22.5m of that loan, while the previous owner Pepco was owed £7.5m.
Gordon Brothers rejected various offers to buy the business as a going concern with deals to pay off that loan.
Irish firm Martin Property Group offered to pay off £5m of the loan up front, and defer the rest of the payments to 2030.
London-based Xyra group offered £12.5m up front but ran out of time to get a deal over the line.
German investment firm Zachert Private Equity is also understood to have made a late offer.
The crisis at Poundland really came to a head over the past few weeks after Gordon Brothers restricted access to funds for day-to-day operations.
This meant that stock at the retailer was not being replenished at the necessary pace in the vital run-up to the festive period.
Are you a Poundland employee? Tell us your story. Get in touch.
